SEED REMOVAL, SEED PREDATION, AND SECONDARY DISPERSAL
S TEPHEN B. V ANDER W ALL , 1 K ELLIE M. K UHN , AND M AURIE J. B ECK
Department of Biology and the Program in Ecology, Evolution and Conservation Biology, University of Nevada, Reno,
Nevada 89557 USA
Abstract. Many studies of postdispersal seed fate use seed removal as an index of seed
predation. However, following primary seed dispersal, some seeds are transported intact
by ants, dung beetles, scatter-hoarding animals, or abiotic processes to new microsites
(secondary dispersal) where germination is possible. Despite a growing realization that
secondary seed dispersal can play an important role in plant recruitment, many researchers
continue to use seed removal as a proxy for seed predation and are focused too intently
on only the initial step of seed fate. We describe, using examples from the recent literature,
how the results of some seed removal studies may have been misinterpreted, present plau-
sible, alternative explanations for the fate of seeds in those studies, and discuss the im-
portance of detailed studies of seed fates. Following the fates of seeds can be difﬁcult, but
such studies contribute much more to our understanding of seed dynamics and plant ﬁtness.
Key words: frugivory; myrmecochory; plant demography; secondary seed dispersal; seed caching;
seed fate; seed predation; seed removal; seed-tracking methods.
I NTRODUCTION
Secondary seed dispersal, any signiﬁcant movement
of viable seeds following initial (primary) dispersal,
has emerged as an important process in the reproduc-
tive cycle of some plants (Chambers and MacMahon
1994, Vander Wall and Longland 2004). Ants, rodents,
birds, dung beetles, and abiotic factors such as wind
and water can move seeds after primary dispersal. Only
since the 1980s have we appreciated the importance of
secondary seed dispersal in the demography of plants.
The view that has emerged is that seed dispersal is
often a multistep process that often incorporates two
or more different means of seed movement. Conse-
quently, it is inappropriate to assume, as many studies
of seed fate have done, that removed seeds have been
consumed by seed predators (e.g., Heithaus 1981, Koll-
mann et al. 1998, Schreiner et al. 2000, Rey et al. 2002,
Moles et al. 2003).
A common methodology in the study of seed fates
is to place a population of seeds on the ground, either
singly or in clumps, and monitor their removal over
time. Removal studies can provide some useful infor-
mation on seed dynamics, but the results of these stud-
ies are often misinterpreted. In an incomplete survey
of the recent literature, we identiﬁed 115 recent papers

that assume, usually with little supporting evidence,
that removed seed had been consumed and that use the
rate of seed removal as a proxy for a measure of seed
predation (K. M. Kuhn, unpublished data). In effect,
seed fate is being deﬁned rather than studied (Levey
and Byrne 1993). To their credit, some seed removal
studies do mention the possibility of secondary dis-
persal (e.g., Hulme and Borelli 1999, Moles et al.
2003), but even these suggest that secondary dispersal
is relatively unlikely, and conclude that seed removal
is essentially seed predation. However, as we learn
more about the complexities of seed fates, we are be-
ginning to realize that, for many plant species, survival
following seed removal is a frequent occurrence. We
argue that, given the growing appreciation of the im-
portance of secondary seed dispersal, we need to be
more careful before making conclusions concerning
seed fates.
P OTENTIAL F ATES OF R EMOVED S EEDS
Seed consumption is a common fate of dispersed
seeds found by animals. Ants, beetles, rodents, birds,
microbes, and a host of other organisms are proﬁcient
at ﬁnding and consuming seeds. However, a number of
animal groups not only move seeds without killing
them, but also transport them to microsites that favor
seedling establishment. Secondary dispersal by ants is
well known and many plants produce seeds with elaio-
802 NOTES Ecology, Vol. 86, No. 3
somes, food bodies attractive to ants, to facilitate this
means of dispersal (e.g., Berg 1975). Ant dispersal of
seeds is sometimes preceded by ballistic dispersal,
which serves to scatter seeds and to reduce seed pre-
dation by other types of animals around the parent (e.g.,
Ohkawara and Higashi 1994). Elaiosome-bearing seeds
can also be dispersed through the feces of birds. The
seed and elaiosome usually survive the short trip
through the bird’s gut, and then ants remove seeds from
feces and carry them back to their nests. For example,
ants (Aphaenogaster swammerdami) secondarily dis-
persed 45% of the seeds of a Malagasy tree (Commi-
phora guillaumini) initially dispersed in the feces of
the Lesser Vasa Parrot (Coracopsis nigra) (Bohning-
Gaese et al. 1999). However, many species of ant-dis-
persed seeds lack elaiosomes. Ants remove seeds from
the feces or regurgitate of birds and feed on remnants
of the fruit pulp (Pizo and Oliveira 1998, Passos and
Oliveira 2002) or eat some of the seeds and store the
rest. Levey and Byrne (1993) reported how leaf-litter
ants (Pheidole spp.) gathered 81% of small seeds from
bird feces, cached ;8–33% in their twig nests, and
deposited an additional 6% in refuse piles. Many of
these seeds germinated directly from cache sites or re-
fuse piles. Levey and Byrne (1993) found 30 species
of intact seeds in Pheidole nebulosa caches and 19
species in refuse piles. None of these seeds had any
apparent adaptations for ant dispersal (e.g., they lacked
elaiosomes).
In recent years, a number of studies have focused on
the importance of dung beetles (Scarabaeine) in sec-
ondary seed dispersal (Estrada and Coates-Estrada
1991, Andresen 2002). The dung of herbivores and
frugivores can contain many seeds. Dung beetles quick-
ly locate fresh dung deposits, transport dung short dis-
tances, and bury it. Some of the dung is buried at depths
that favor seed germination and seedling emergence.
Estrada and Coates-Estrada (1991) found that in pro-
tected plots, 44% of buried seeds germinated and es-
tablished seedlings, whereas in unprotected plots (open
to foraging rodents that acted as seed predators or sec-
ondary dispersers of seeds) 14% of seed established
seedlings. Because dung beetles are widely distributed
throughout temperate and tropical regions, it is likely
that this mode of secondary dispersal will eventually
prove to be very widespread and important.
Secondary dispersal of seeds and nuts by food-stor-
ing rodents and corvids is a well-studied phenomenon.
Many of the plants that are dispersed in this way drop
seeds or nuts at maturity to facilitate seed harvest by
ground-foraging animals (Forget 1996, Peres and Baid-
er 1997, Yasuda et al. 2000, Vander Wall 2001, Jansen
and den Ouden 2004). Although many of these seeds
and nuts are eaten, a large percentage is scatter-hoard-
ed. For example, rodents cached at least 56–77% of
Jeffrey pine (Pinus jeffreyi) seeds that were initially
arranged around three trees in patterns that simulated
primary dispersal by wind (Vander Wall 2002). Seed-
caching rodents also remove seeds from the feces of
large mammals and birds (Forget and Milleron 1991,
Wenny 1999, Feer and Forget 2002). This plant–animal
interaction is geographically widespread, but second-
ary dispersal of seeds by food-caching animals is not
well documented in Australia and Africa. However,
several species of marsupial and placental mammals
have been found to be avid scatter-hoarders and effec-
tive dispersers of plant seeds in Australia (Thiemer
2001, Dennis 2003), and scatter-hoarding of seeds may
also prove to be an important means of seed dispersal
in south Africa (e.g., Midgley et al. 2002). More re-
search is likely to reveal that scatter-hoarding is a wide-
spread behavior and an important means of seed dis-
persal in many temperate and tropical habitats.
Abiotic processes also redistribute seeds on the sur-
face of the ground or transport seeds into the soil seed
bank. Wind moves seeds across the ground or snow,
and rain splash and sheet ﬂow of water across the
ground are known to move seeds (Matlack 1989, John-
son and Fryer 1992, Grifﬁth and Forseth 2002).
I NTERPRETATION OF S EED R EMOVAL S TUDIES
In a recent study of seed removal in which seed
predation was inferred, Moles et al. (2003) examined
the rate of postdispersal seed predation of 81 seed spe-
cies in three different ecosystems in New South Wales,
Australia, by monitoring seeds placed along seed re-
moval transects. We examined the list of species used
in the Moles et al. (2003) study (Ecological Archives
E084-083-A5–A7) and identiﬁed eight species of
known myrmecochores, including Boronia ledifolia
and Phebalium squamulosum (Rutaceae), Dodonea tri-
quetra (Sapindaceae), and Pomaderris ferruginea
(Rhamnaceae) at the Sturt National Park site (Berg
1975, Rice and Westoby 1981, Auld 2001); Dissocar-
pus biﬂorus, Sclerolaena convexula, and Sclerolaena
diacantha (Chenopodiaceae) at Ku-ring-gai Chase Na-
tional Park (Davidson and Morton 1981); and Mono-
toca elliptica (Epacridaceae) at Kosciuszko National
Park (Rice and Westoby 1981). For these eight species
(and perhaps others), ants may have removed seeds and
taken them to their nests. This is a critically important
distinction because for myrmecochores, seed removal
by ants is an essential step toward successful repro-
duction. Moles et al. (2003) also compiled data from
46 studies of seed removal that included 280 plant spe-
cies (Ecological Archives E084–083-A9). Most of
these studies equated seed removal to seed predation
without supporting evidence of actual seed fate. Some
of these studies (e.g., Ohkawara and Higashi 1994, For-
get 1996, Peres and Baider 1997) were actually detailed
March 2005 803NOTES
investigations of secondary seed dispersal that were
misinterpreted as seed predation by Moles et al. (2003).
For example, Moles et al. (2003) listed Carapa procera
seed removal as predation despite the fact that Forget
(1996) found that 25–48% of seed removed by rodents
were scatter-hoarded and 9–43% were eaten.
Blate et al. (1998) monitored the removal of 40 spe-
cies of seeds in Kalimantan, Indonesia. Among these
species was Lithocarpus sp. (Fagaceae), which pro-
duces large (8.1-g) acorns. Lithocarpus, like most other
members of this large family, is known to be dispersed
by seed-caching rodents and corvids (Vander Wall
2001). Mature acorns fall to the ground and removal
is an essential step in the dispersal process; acorns that
are not quickly removed die or are eaten by animals
that offer no prospect of dispersal. In Kalimantan (is-
land of Borneo), a number of food-caching rodents,
such as Leopoldamys, Maxomys, Niviventer, and Lar-
iscus (Yasuda et al. 2000, Zhang et al. 2004), could
have removed and buried the nuts. The other 39 plant
species in the sample had ﬂeshy fruits and seeds dis-
persed by frugivorous birds. Clear evidence of con-
sumption was noted in only 26% of removal events
(mean for all species). Seed mass ranged from 0.1 g
to 11.6 g. The smaller seeds might be attractive to ants
or moved by dung beetles. Scatter-hoarding by rodents
and corvids in this part of the world is not well studied,
but we suspect that many of the medium-to-large seeds
would be attractive to scatter-hoarding animals that re-
move the seeds from feces (Vander Wall and Longland
2004). For example, Wenny (1999) found that scatter-
hoarding rodents secondarily dispersed Guarea glabra
and Guarea kunthiana seeds in Costa Rica. The seeds
are consumed by birds (primary dispersers) and re-
gurgitated. Agoutis (Dasyprocta punctata) and other
rodents gathered the seeds and cached 45.6% and
26.6%, respectively. Removal of Brazil nuts (Berthol-
letia excelsa, Lecythidaceae) is largely by scatter-
hoarding agoutis (Dasyprocta) (Peres and Baider
1997), and this species interaction is considered es-
sential for the long-term maintenance of these impor-
tant trees in neotropical rain forests (Peres et al. 2003).
These three plant species were included in the com-
pilation of Moles et al. (2003) as examples of seed
predation.
Boman and Casper (1995) equated postdispersal seed
removal to predation in their study of six plant species
in hardwood forests of eastern Pennsylvania, USA.
Among the species they studied were beech (Fagus
grandifolia) and oaks (Quercus sp.), plants known to
be dispersed by nut-caching jays and rodents. Boman
and Casper (1995) also included ﬂowering dogwood
(Cornus ﬂorida), a seed dispersed by frugivorous birds,
in their sample. S. B. Vander Wall, K. M. Kuhn, and
J. R. Gworek (unpublished data) found that rodents
removed the seeds of Cornus stolonifera from bird fe-
ces and cached them. A similar process may be oc-
curring in eastern hardwood forests.
McCarthy (1994) found that 85–100% of mockernut
hickory (Carya tomentosa, Juglandaceae) nuts (n 5
300) cached under leaf litter were removed within 5
days, and he attributed this to gray squirrels (Sciurus
carolinensis). He concluded that postdispersal seed
predation was a major force limiting recruitment, al-
though he did not report any evidence that the nuts had
actually been eaten. However, squirrels and other ro-
dents routinely recache items that they have pilfered,
so it was more likely that nuts had simply been redis-
tributed rather than consumed. Hau (1997) monitored
the removal of Quercus, Lithocarpus, and Castanopsis
(Fagaceae) nuts on degraded hillsides in Hong Kong,
China, by rodents (very likely Niviventer and Rattus)
and considered removal to be seed predation. However,
Zhang et al. (2004) report that Niviventer and Rattus
are important agents of nut dispersal at several sites in
China.
Several authors have studied the removal of Prunus
stones (Rosaceae) (including P. annularis, P. virgini-
ana, P. avium, P. spinosa, and P. tumeriana) by rodents
(Webb and Willson 1985, Osunkoya 1994, Holl and
Lulow 1997, Kollmann et al. 1998). Although some
authors acknowledged that rodents might have cached
removed stones, they assumed that most seeds had
probably been eaten, despite the fact that only ;5% of
the seed stations had evidence of on-site seed con-
sumption. However, Zhang and Wang (2001) found that
seed-storing rodents dispersed the stones of Prunus ar-
meniaca, and M. J. Beck and S. B. Vander Wall (un-
published data) found that rodents routinely scatter-
hoarded the stones of Prunus virginiana, P. andersonii,
P. emarginata, and P. fasciculata, many of which suc-
cessfully germinated and established.
Ohkawara and Higashi (1994) described how two
species of Viola are dispersed by a combination of
ballistic dispersal followed by myrmecochory. Ants
gather the elaiosome-bearing seeds, carry them to their
nests, consume the elaiosome, and dump the seeds in
a refuse pile where many germinate and establish
plants. Moles et al. (2003) attributed this ant removal
to seed predation. Myster (1997) observed the removal
of Miconia racemosa seeds by Pheidole ants at La Sel-
va Biological Station in Costa Rica and attributed this
removal to seed predators without conﬁrming seed
fates. However, Levey and Byrne (1993) found that
removed Miconia nervosa and Miconia centrodesma
seeds at La Selva were being dispersed by Pheidole
ants.
The potential for secondary seed dispersal by dung
beetles is often underestimated in studies of seed re-
moval. Those studying seed removal often gather seeds
804 NOTES Ecology, Vol. 86, No. 3
by hand, remove structures that would normally be lost
during seed dispersal (e.g., fruit pulp), and set them
out along transects. However, if seeds normally would
be incorporated into bird feces or mammal dung during
dispersal (e.g., Janzen 1982), the atypical treatment that
they receive from experimenters would lower the
seeds’ probability of removal by dung beetles. For ex-
ample, seeds in dung might be removed quickly by
dispersers, whereas similar clean seeds would be ig-
nored by dung beetles and exposed to increased risk
from seed predators. An experiment with cleaned seeds
might lead one to conclude, incorrectly, that potential
secondary dispersers are ineffective at moving seeds
while overestimating the rate of predation. Seed re-
moval is context dependent, and to fairly evaluate hy-
potheses of postdispersal seed predation vs. secondary
dispersal, one must present seeds in a manner that sim-
ulates natural processes.
A N A LTERNATIVE A PPROACH
Postdispersal seed removal can be seed predation,
but it can also represent the next step in a multistep
seed dispersal process. The truth is that, for most spe-
cies, we simply do not know what proportions of sec-
ondarily dispersed seeds are eaten, survive intact, or
suffer other fates. Chambers and MacMahon (1994)
reviewed the literature on seed fates and concluded that
the latter phases of seed dispersal are likely to have at
least as great an impact on the patterning of plants in
communities as the ﬁrst phase. Vander Wall and Long-
land (2004) examined the beneﬁts of diplochory (two-
phase seed dispersal in which each phase is carried out
by a different mechanism) in ﬁve dispersal syndromes
and concluded that the primary beneﬁts of phase one
dispersal are usually predator escape and colonization
of new patches, whereas the primary beneﬁts of phase
two dispersal are usually predator escape and directed
dispersal. Through directed dispersal, plants attempt to
deliver seeds to microsites where seedling establish-
ment is likely to be successful. These reviews suggest
that secondary dispersal provides important beneﬁts to
plants, and if we aim to understand the adaptive value
of seed dispersal, the fate of seeds after initial dispersal
cannot be ignored.
We ﬁnd the widespread assumption that removed
seeds have been consumed by seed predators to be
unwarranted for two reasons. First, such incorrect as-
sumptions result in the accumulation of unreliable
knowledge (Romesburg 1981). A number of studies
(e.g., Whelan et al. 1991, Hulme 1997, Kollmann et
al. 1998, Hulme and Hunt 1999, Rey et al. 2002, Moles
et al. 2003) have justiﬁed their assumption that removal
equals predation because others have done so in the
past. Some studies (e.g., Schupp 1990, Holl and Lulow
1997, Pizo 1997, Alcantara et al. 2000, Schreiner et al.
2000, Obeso and Fernandez-Calvo 2002) report that
the levels of ‘‘predation’’ that they have observed are
comparable to those reported by others and then cite
studies that have made the same assumption that seed
removal equals predation. Unfortunately, much of the
research on postdispersal seed predation needs to be
reassessed and, when found wanting, repeated, using
methods that actually track the fate of seeds. Second,
assuming that removed seeds are dead causes research-
ers to miss potentially important events in the seed
dispersal process. Some authors seem to assume that
even though not all removed seeds are consumed, seed
removal is strongly correlated with seed predation and
therefore is a useful estimate of seed predation. This
may often be true, but the presumption of mortality
obscures important events of seed escape and dispersal,
whether common or rare. Even if death is the most
common consequence of seed removal, the few seeds
that survive are the ones that drive plant recruitment
(Levey and Byrne 1993). If we hope to understand the
details of plant recruitment, we need to determine how
often seeds escape predation, how this occurs, and what
are the fates of these seeds. Ignorance of the details of
postdispersal seed fates prevents a clear understanding
of the factors determining plant establishment and the
nature of seed–disperser coevolution. We need to re-
focus our efforts from monitoring seed removal to fol-
lowing removed seeds to their ultimate demise or suc-
cessful germination and establishment. The many al-
ternative pathways that seeds follow between initial
dispersal and their ultimate fate are much more difﬁcult
to study than simple seed removal, but such studies
contribute much more to our understanding of seed
dynamics and plant ﬁtness. To understand how natural
selection shapes seed and fruit traits such as size, mor-
phology, chemical composition, and germination
schedules, we need to understand better why some
seeds fail while others succeed.
Over the past 15 years, a number of techniques have
been developed for tracking seeds reliably. Many of
these have been described and evaluated by Forget and
Wenny (2004). Large seeds and nuts can be followed
using various line and tag methods (e.g., Forget and
Milleron 1991), whereas small seeds can be tracked
using isotopes and ﬂuorescent dyes (e.g., Longland and
Clements 1995, Longland et al. 2001). These methods
can be used in conjunction with remote cameras to
conﬁrm the identity of animals removing seeds (Yasuda
et al. 2000, Jansen and Den Ouden 2004). Following
seeds is a challenging, but not an intractable, problem,
but despite all of the difﬁculties, it is the only sure way
to gain reliable knowledge of seed fates. Meanwhile,
and in the absence of such detailed studies of seed fate,
it would be appropriate to label postdispersal seed re-
March 2005 805NOTES
moval as just that, and to take greater care in describing
the consequences of such removal.
